title: Helm Chart Authoring
summary: Installing charts is easy. Writing them — creating reusable, configurable, well-structured charts that your team can actually maintain — requires understanding the template engine, named templates, and Helm's opinionated conventions.

sections.title: Chart structure and conventions
sections.body:
## What Helm Charts Are and Why Structure Matters

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A Helm **chart** is a collection of files that together describe a set of Kubernetes resources — a deployment, service, ingress, HPA, config maps, secrets — needed to run an application. The chart's job is to make a complex, multi-resource application installable with a single command and configurable without editing YAML by hand.

**Why Helm exists:** Kubernetes manifests are powerful but repetitive and environment-specific. Deploying the same application to development, staging, and production requires the same set of resources but with different replica counts, resource limits, image tags, and domain names. Without Helm, teams maintain separate copies of their manifests per environment — or write fragile `sed` one-liners to substitute values. Helm solves this with a template engine and a values system: one set of templates, many configurations.

**The chart vs the release:** A chart is the template (like a class in programming). A release is a specific instantiation of that chart installed into a cluster (like an instance). You can install the same chart twice in the same cluster — for example, once as `myapp-prod` and once as `myapp-staging` — and Helm manages them as separate releases.

**The `values.yaml` contract:** This file is the public API of your chart. Operators customize behavior by providing their own values files that override the defaults. Every value that you want to be overridable must have a default in `values.yaml`. Values that exist in templates but are not in `values.yaml` are invisible to users of the chart, which is a documentation failure as much as a design one.

**Convention-driven structure:** Helm imposes a specific directory layout because the tooling depends on it. `templates/` holds all Kubernetes manifest templates. `_helpers.tpl` holds named template definitions (the leading underscore tells Helm not to render it as a manifest). `charts/` holds dependencies. Deviating from this layout breaks `helm lint`, `helm template`, and packaging. Following it means any Helm user can navigate your chart immediately.

**`Chart.yaml` has two version fields** that serve different purposes: `version` is the chart version (increment this when you change the chart structure or defaults), and `appVersion` is the version of the application the chart deploys (a documentation field, not enforced by Helm). Both follow semantic versioning conventions.

```
my-app/
  Chart.yaml          # chart metadata
  values.yaml         # default values
  templates/
    _helpers.tpl      # named templates (reusable snippets)
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    ingress.yaml
    configmap.yaml
    hpa.yaml
    serviceaccount.yaml
    NOTES.txt         # printed after helm install
  charts/             # sub-charts (dependencies)
```

```yaml
# Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: my-app
description: My application Helm chart
type: application
version: 0.1.0        # chart version (semver)
appVersion: "1.2.3"   # application version (for reference)

dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: "19.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: redis.enabled  # only install if redis.enabled=true
```

```yaml
# values.yaml — all defaults here
replicaCount: 2

image:
  repository: my-registry/my-app
  tag: ""           # default empty — override in CI
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 8080

ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: public
  host: my-app.example.com
  tls: true

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    memory: 256Mi   # no CPU limit — avoid throttling

autoscaling:
  enabled: false
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70

redis:
  enabled: false
```

sections.title: The Helm template engine
sections.body:
## How Helm Templates Work: Go Templates and Sprig

Helm's template engine is Go's `text/template` package, extended with the Sprig function library. If you have never worked with Go templates, the `{{ }}` syntax can look unfamiliar at first, but the model is straightforward: any text inside double curly braces is evaluated as an expression; everything outside is passed through as-is.

**The dot (`.`) is the current scope.** When Helm renders a template, it passes in a data object that contains everything available to the template: `.Values` (your values.yaml data), `.Release` (metadata about this Helm release), `.Chart` (metadata from Chart.yaml), and `.Files` (access to non-template files). The dot at the end of `include "my-app.labels" .` passes the current scope into the named template — if you omit it, the included template cannot access any of these objects.

**Whitespace control is critical in YAML.** A Go template that emits an extra blank line or unexpected indentation will produce invalid YAML that Kubernetes rejects. The `-` in `{{-` strips all whitespace (including newlines) before the expression; `-}}` strips whitespace after. The `nindent N` function adds a leading newline and indents by N spaces, which is the standard way to embed multi-line template output inside a YAML structure. Getting whitespace wrong is the most common source of `helm template` errors.

**`toYaml | nindent`** is the standard pattern for embedding entire YAML sub-trees — like the `resources` block — from values into templates. `toYaml` serializes the Go map to YAML text; `nindent` applies the correct indentation for where the block appears in the manifest. This lets users specify arbitrarily nested resource configurations in `values.yaml` without the chart author needing to template each field individually.

**Conditional inclusion with `{{- if }}`** is how charts support optional features. An ingress resource should only be created if the user enables it. An HPA should only exist if autoscaling is enabled. Wrapping entire resource blocks in `{{- if .Values.feature.enabled }}` means the resource is completely absent from the rendered output when disabled — not present with zero replicas or empty fields, but entirely omitted.

**`default`** provides fallback values inline in the template. `{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}` means: use the user-supplied tag if set, otherwise fall back to the chart's declared appVersion. This pattern lets users override specific values without needing to set every value explicitly.

Helm uses Go's text/template engine with Sprig functions. The syntax is `{{ }}` for expressions.

```yaml
# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "my-app.fullname" . }}
  namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }}
  labels:
    {{- include "my-app.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  {{- end }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "my-app.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "my-app.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
        imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}
        ports:
        - containerPort: {{ .Values.service.port }}
        resources:
          {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 10 }}
        env:
        - name: ENV
          value: {{ .Values.env | default "production" | quote }}
        {{- if .Values.extraEnv }}
        {{- toYaml .Values.extraEnv | nindent 8 }}
        {{- end }}
```

**Key template functions:**

```
{{ .Values.key }}          access values
{{ .Release.Name }}        release name
{{ .Release.Namespace }}   namespace
{{ .Chart.AppVersion }}    from Chart.yaml
default "fallback" .x     use fallback if x is empty
quote                      wrap in quotes
nindent N                  indent N spaces + leading newline
toYaml                     serialize to YAML
{{- ... -}}               strip whitespace before/after
if / else / end
range                      iterate over list or map
with                       change scope
```

sections.title: Named templates in _helpers.tpl
Values override patterns for environments
sections.body:
## Managing Environment-Specific Configuration Without Duplication

One of Helm's core value propositions is the ability to deploy the same application to multiple environments with different configurations. A staging deployment might run 2 replicas with small resource limits; production runs 10 replicas with larger limits, autoscaling enabled, and TLS on the ingress. Without Helm, this means maintaining separate YAML files that diverge over time. With Helm, you maintain one set of templates and one `values.yaml` per environment.

**The values layer model:** Helm merges values files in the order they are specified, with later files taking precedence. `helm install my-app ./my-app -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml` loads the base defaults from `values.yaml`, then overlays only the fields present in `values-prod.yaml`. The result is that `values-prod.yaml` is small and focused — it contains only the differences from the defaults, not a full copy. This makes it easy to see exactly what makes production different.

**`--set` vs values files:** The `--set key=value` flag overrides individual values at the command line. It is convenient for one-off changes and for CI pipelines that inject the image tag at deploy time (`--set image.tag=$SHA`). However, `--set` values are not committed to version control, making them invisible in the audit trail. For permanent environment differences, always use a values file. Reserve `--set` for dynamic values like image tags and timestamps.

**`helm template` is your primary development tool.** It renders templates to stdout without connecting to any cluster. This is how you validate your templates during development: run `helm template` locally, inspect the output, and fix template errors before deploying. Combined with `helm lint`, which checks for structural and semantic errors in the chart, you catch most mistakes before they reach a cluster.

**The ArgoCD integration** shows why Helm authoring skills matter even for teams using GitOps. ArgoCD natively understands Helm charts — you point an Application at a Helm chart repository or a local chart path, provide values files and parameter overrides, and ArgoCD renders the templates and syncs the output. The values files are stored in Git, so every configuration change goes through a pull request.

```bash norun
# Override at install time
helm install my-app ./my-app \
    --set image.tag=v1.2.3 \
    --set replicaCount=3

# Better: use values files per environment
helm install my-app ./my-app \
    -f values.yaml \
    -f values-prod.yaml     # prod overrides, applied last

# values-prod.yaml — only prod-specific overrides
replicaCount: 5

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi
  limits:
    memory: 1Gi

autoscaling:
  enabled: true
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20

ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: my-app.prod.example.com
  tls: true
```

```bash norun
# Render templates locally (no cluster needed)
helm template my-release ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml

# Lint for errors
helm lint ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml

# Diff what would change (with helm-diff plugin)
helm diff upgrade my-app ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml

# With ArgoCD — values files in your Helm app
# In your ArgoCD Application:
spec:
  source:
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values.yaml
        - values-prod.yaml
      parameters:
        - name: image.tag
          value: v1.2.3
```

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.body:
## Quick Reference for Chart Authors

This reference covers the commands and template constructs you will reach for repeatedly when authoring and maintaining Helm charts. Treat it as a lookup companion to the detailed sections above — the concepts behind each item are explained there.

**Workflow summary for chart development:**

1. `helm create` scaffolds a complete, working chart with sensible defaults. Start here rather than from scratch.
2. Edit templates and values, then `helm template` to inspect rendered output. Iterate until the YAML looks correct.
3. `helm lint` to catch structural and schema errors — this runs automatically in most CI pipelines.
4. `helm install --dry-run` to simulate an install against a real cluster (validates server-side but does not apply).
5. `helm upgrade --install` for idempotent deploys — installs if the release does not exist, upgrades if it does.
6. `helm diff upgrade` (requires the helm-diff plugin) to see exactly what a `helm upgrade` would change before running it. This is the Helm equivalent of `terraform plan`.

**Named template discipline:** Keep all `define` blocks in `_helpers.tpl`. Never define templates in regular manifest files — they work but become impossible to find. Use a consistent naming prefix (`chart-name.helper-name`) to avoid collisions with dependency chart helpers.

**Whitespace rules to memorize:** Use `{{-` (dash on left) at the start of most template actions to strip the preceding newline. Use `| nindent N` (not `indent N`) when you need a leading newline before the indented block — which is almost always the case when embedding blocks inside YAML structures.

```bash norun
# ── Chart authoring commands ──────────────────────
helm create my-app            # scaffold a new chart
helm lint ./my-app            # validate chart
helm template release ./my-app # render templates locally
helm template ... --debug     # show computed values too
helm package ./my-app         # create .tgz for distribution

# ── Template functions ────────────────────────────
.Values.key                   access a value
default "val" .Values.key     fallback if empty
quote / squote                wrap in double/single quotes
toYaml | nindent 4           serialize + indent
trimSuffix "-" | trunc 63    truncate and trim (for names)
printf "%s-%s" .A .B          string format
upper / lower / title         case conversion
contains "x" .Values.str     substring check
if .Values.enabled ... end    conditional
range .Values.list ... end    iterate

# ── Built-in objects ──────────────────────────────
.Release.Name                 release name
.Release.Namespace            target namespace
.Release.IsInstall / .IsUpgrade
.Chart.Name / .AppVersion / .Version
.Values.*                     from values.yaml

# ── Named templates ───────────────────────────────
{{- define "chart.helper" -}}  # define in _helpers.tpl
  content
{{- end }}
{{- include "chart.helper" . }}  # use anywhere

# ── Whitespace control ────────────────────────────
{{- ... -}}  strip whitespace/newlines on both sides
{{- ... }}   strip before only (most common)
```

sections.title: Quiz
sections.body:
## Check Your Understanding

Helm authoring combines YAML knowledge, Go template syntax, and Kubernetes resource semantics. The questions below focus on the areas where misunderstandings cause real production problems: whitespace handling, label mutability, and the distinction between `_helpers.tpl` and regular templates.

For the terminal exercise, use the sandbox's live Helm and Kubernetes setup to explore real chart output. Looking at the rendered manifest of a running chart is one of the fastest ways to internalize how templates, values, and named templates interact in practice. Pay attention to label consistency across the Deployment, Service, and any other resources — that consistency is what named templates in `_helpers.tpl` guarantee.

**Q1.** What does `{{- include "my-app.labels" . | nindent 4 }}` do, and why the `-` before `include`?

**Q2.** What's the difference between selector labels and regular labels, and why does it matter?

**Q3.** You want to conditionally include a block only when `ingress.enabled` is true. Write the template syntax.

**Q4.** Why is `_helpers.tpl` prefixed with `_`?

---

**Answers:**

**A1.** `include` renders the named template `my-app.labels` with `.` (current context). `nindent 4` adds a newline and indents by 4 spaces (needed to fit inside YAML structure). The `-` strips the leading whitespace/newline before the `include`, preventing an extra blank line.

**A2.** Selector labels (`matchLabels`) are used by the Service and Deployment to find pods. They **cannot change after first install** — Kubernetes rejects changes to immutable selector fields. Regular labels are metadata only and can be updated freely. Always keep selectors minimal and stable.

**A3.**
```yaml
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
# ...
{{- end }}
```

**A4.** Files starting with `_` are not rendered as Kubernetes manifests — Helm skips them. They're only used for `define` blocks that other templates `include`.

---

**Exercise:**

```bash
# In the terminal, explore helm template output
helm template my-release . 2>/dev/null || echo 'no chart here'

# Try with the mock helm
helm list
helm get values argocd
helm get manifest argocd

# Check chart structure of argocd:
helm get manifest argocd | head -30
```
